transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-06-25
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~75 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Patel (Redwood AE), Alex Chen (Redwood SE), Riley Park (Redwood SE), Dr. Maya Rao (NovaHealth CTO), Samir Gupta (NovaHealth ML Eng), Priya Nair (NovaHealth Infra)

[00:00] Jordan: hey everyone thanks for joining, um we'll do a deep dive today on 128k long context performance, alex's going to lead on runtime details and we'll surface tradeoffs for Dedicated vs hosted vs VPC. quick intros?
[00:17] Dr. Maya: maya here, CTO at NovaHealth. we're investigating ingesting full patient histories and imaging meta into a single context for summarization and clinical QA. main constraints are latency under 2s for short queries, and ability to run on-prem for PHI.
[00:32] Samir: samir, ml eng, we'll own dataset prep and evals. we care about throughput — we expect bursts of 200 concurrent small queries against a large context. cost is also a big factor.
[00:47] Priya: priya infra, we need VPC peering, KMS/HSM integration, and audit logs. SOC 2 is a must.
[00:55] Alex: great; quick agenda — kernel/attention optimizations for 128k, kv cache behavior across chunked prompts, batching strategies and latency tradeoffs, quantization impacts on perf and accuracy, and deployment options VPC/on-prem.

--- Summary and early technical notes ---
[03:10] Alex: so at a high level, 128k context is mostly about memory and attention compute. we typically don't run full O(n^2) attention at 128k; we use chunked attention windows, sliding attention, and sparse/longformer-style attention to keep compute linear-ish. for Redwood runtime we have optimized kernels for sustained KV cache streaming and attention tiling, but the model architecture matters — some open models are patched to support 128k natively, others need compiler/graph rewrites.
[03:45] Samir: can you explain more on "kv cache streaming"? we've seen K-V cash uh in other docs, but behavior when you stitch chunks is fuzzy.
[04:05] Alex: yeah, kv cache streaming is the technique where instead of re-encoding the entire context you append chunks to the KV cache and only compute attention for the new tokens plus the sliding window. practically you get big savings. caveat: when you do chunking you lose some cross-chunk attention unless you overlap chunks or run a second-pass global attention. that second pass can be expensive.
[04:40] Riley: (interruption) and we see folks use a hybrid: local chunked attention for most tokens and periodic global attention markers for critical tokens e.g., tags or summaries. that reduces compute while keeping global coherence.
[05:05] Dr. Maya: so for clinical QA we need cross-document references, like lab reference referencing earlier notes. would the hybrid approach handle that?
[05:20] Alex: Depends on how often cross-reference occurs. if it's rare, you can run local attention primarily and then trigger a global pass on a short prefix of important tokens (like headings, patient id, key events). if it's frequent you'd want a wider overlap or models that natively support sparse global attention.

--- Timestamps showing perf numbers and rough benchmarking ---
[08:00] Alex: with our Atlas-optimized runtime (note: not perfect transcript, we said Atlas in earlier decks but internal name) on an A100-like instance, a 128k forward for sampling one token with fully streaming KV (no global pass) can be in the ~600-900ms range for a single request if you tune batching small. With dedicated pools and kernel fusions we can push tail latency down — but it's highly sensitive to sequence length distribution and batch size.
[08:45] Samir: can you quantify throughput for concurrent small queries? we mentioned 200 concurrent.
[09:05] Alex: throughput is a batching story. If you aim for sub-second latency you often keep batch sizes small which reduces throughput. For 200 concurrent small queries, the platform can autoscale dedicated GPUs and split across shards; throughput in tokens/sec can be higher but cost rises. For example, with moderate batching we saw effective throughput 3x-5x higher vs very low batch. tradeoff: average latency increases.

--- Batching strategies and latency tradeoffs ---
[11:30] Alex: recommended patterns: 1) For low-latency interactive paths, use small batch sizes, prefix caching and a hot-worker pool. 2) For high-throughput background jobs, use larger batching and quantized models. 3) Mixed: route by policy — e.g., SLO route to dedicated hot pool, fallback to cheaper quantized pool for noncritical queries.
[12:04] Priya: what about prefix caching? we have many repeated prefixes — patient header templates etc. How does Redwood's prefix cache work?
[12:20] Alex: Prefix caching stores KV entries for common prefixes so new queries that reuse them avoid recomputing the attention for those tokens. It reduces cost dramatically when there's reuse. caveat — cache cold-start and invalidation when you roll models. Also encryption at rest for cache snapshots in VPC mode is supported.
[12:45] Riley: note, per-token accounting in console will show you savings from cache hits so you can tune.

--- Quantization and accuracy tradeoffs ---
[15:30] Samir: curious about 4-bit vs 8-bit quant. do you see big quality regressions on clinical text?
[15:48] Alex: quantization depends heavily on model and eval set. Many LLMs are robust to 8-bit (INT8 or Q8) with minimal quality loss; 4-bit (QLoRA style/experimental kernels) can introduce drift on certain reasoning tasks. For clinical QA I'd recommend running eval sets. Our Optimize tool can sweep quantization and show delta in Rouge/Exact Match on your prompts.
[16:20] Dr. Maya: if we do quantization for cost, can we route sensitive queries to non-quantized Dedicated nodes and bulk queries to quantized?
[16:32] Jordan: yes, that's the typical hybrid approach. route by label or endpoint. we can set policy in the console.

--- VPC / on-prem constraints ---
[18:10] Priya: for on-prem or VPC, how much of the runtime lives in customer env vs managed control plane? and what about HSM/KMS for keys?
[18:30] Alex: Redwood Private offers a customer-managed control plane option. inference runtime can sit in your VPC or on-prem cluster (we deploy a runtime agent). Keys stay in your KMS or HSM, we support KMS integrations and HSM-backed signing. Audit logs are emit-able to your SIEM over the peered network. There are additional ops considerations: GPU driver versions, NIC RDMA for multi-node KV sharing, and local orchestration.
[19:05] Priya: RDMA — we use on-prem Mellanox, will the runtime leverage NVLink/RDMA?
[19:18] Alex: yes, our Dedicated/on-prem runtime supports NVLink and RDMA for model sharding and KV exchange, but you'll need matching kernel modules and driver versions; we'll share a compatibility matrix.

--- Chunking strategies detailed discussion ---
[24:00] Riley: chunking approaches: fixed-size chunks with overlap, semantic chunking (split by sections/headings), and dynamic chunking (by token importance). Fixed-size is simple but may cut entities; semantic chunking preserves structure but needs good splitter. We often recommend a hybrid: semantic chunking with small overlaps (128-512 tokens) and a periodic global summary token that gets appended to the KV cache.
[24:34] Samir: we use clinical notes separated by date, might be natural chunks. how to preserve cross-note references?
[24:45] Alex: use an index-level retriever that pulls top-K relevant chunks into a working context. For strict single-pass 128k ingest, you can create a document-level summary stream that feeds into a compact global context. If you must keep raw tokens, increase overlap or run a global-attention pass at the end.

--- Attention optimizations and compiler/kernel notes ---
[29:50] Alex: compiler can transform attention into tiled matmuls, fuse softmax ops, and reduce memory copies. Redwood's runtime picks kernels based on seq len and hardware. for example, at 128k we use streaming block attention where we keep only a sliding KV buffer on GPU and spill extended KV to host or NVMe as needed. spill policies matter a lot: if you spill too often you hit IO latency.
[30:20] Samir: does Redwood do automatic NVMe spill? can we tune thresholds?
[30:30] Alex: yes we support NVMe spill for extremely long contexts; thresholds are configurable per-workload. we recommend keeping working set in GPU for latency-sensitive paths. we'll share best-practice configs.

--- Real-world tradeoff examples ---
[34:00] Alex: example scenario: 1) Host short interactive queries against a 128k context where you need <1s tail. You should precompute semantic indices, keep hot prefixes in KV cache, and have a small hot pool of GPUs per region. 2) For nightly batch summarization over 10k docs into a 128k context you can run quantized models with large batch sizes and accept higher latency.
[34:40] Jordan: can we talk cost-ballpark? NovaHealth wants a sense of Dedicated vs hosted.
[34:55] Alex: rough: Hosted (pay-as-you-go) is higher per-token but no infra ops. Dedicated reserved GPUs amortize cost — for steady high throughput it's cheaper. VPC/on-prem has an infra premium for deployment and support. we'll provide a tailored estimate after we see sample usage patterns.

--- Benchmarks and shared artifacts references ---
[39:00] Jordan: i'll drop the benchmark sheet link in the follow-up and we've got a short deck for the runtime optimizations — https://redwood.app/decks/128k-deep-dive (internal link) and a perf spreadsheet: https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/benchmark-128k-sample (shared).
[39:22] Samir: perfect. we'll populate sample docs and a small eval harness.

--- Questions and edge cases ---
[44:10] Dr. Maya: what happens on model upgrades when we rely on cached KV snapshots? invalidation strategy?
[44:30] Alex: rolling model upgrades will invalidate cache. we recommend version-pin critical endpoints or warm the cache during a canary rollout. Redwood supports cache warmers and pre-warm strategies.
[44:52] Priya: if we need encryption-in-use (confidential computing), any support?
[45:05] Alex: we have integrations roadmap for confidential VMs and SGX-style enclaves, but typically HSM + VPC private networks cover most compliance needs. we'll share the roadmap notes.

--- Closing and Recap ---
[58:00] Jordan: recap — action items: send benchmark template, run pilot, NovaHealth to provide infra constraints. target follow-up the week of 2026-07-08, aim to run initial pilot by 2026-07-03.
[58:20] Dr. Maya: sounds good. one ask: include a sample cost model for Dedicated + VPC with 99.9 SLO.
[58:30] Jordan: will do.
[58:40] Samir: thanks alex this was super helpful.
[58:45] Alex: thanks all. we'll email the artifacts and next steps.
[59:00] Speaker 1: (unclear) yep thanks everyone bye.

End of transcript.
